messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Layla, a 51-year-old social ministry worker, had spent decades building a life that kept her busy, useful, and most importantly, never still. She worked at a community outreach center in a bustling part of the city, coordinating food drives and visiting homebound elders. On paper, she was competent and dedicated. But her colleagues had noticed that Layla always chose a seat with a clear line of sight to the nearest exit, and that she would abruptly end one-on-one meetings to grab a coffee for herself and her visitor—an excuse to keep the office door open and to ensure she was never truly alone with another person.

The roots of this vigilance lay in a childhood she had never spoken about in full. Her father, a stern and devout man, had disciplined her with his hands and a leather belt, often in the small back room of their apartment. She remembered the way the room would darken as he closed the door, the smell of dust and his sweat. But when she tried to describe it now, words failed her. She could only feel the memory in her body: sometimes, without warning, her arms would curl protectively over her head, her knees would pull up to her chest, and she would find herself in a tight ball on the floor of her own kitchen, her heart pounding as if she were still a frightened child in that back room. The rage that followed was immediate and overwhelming—a hot, wordless fury that left her shaking and ashamed afterward. She couldn't explain to anyone why she sometimes screamed at her own empty apartment, or why she had to fight the urge to hit the wall.

Avoidance had become her lifeline. She avoided going to the center on days when she knew she would have to lead a small group alone; she called in sick or rearranged schedules. Over time, she began to dread even the thought of work. When she did go, her eyes darted to the corners of the room, and she frequently looked behind her as she walked from her car to the building, certain someone was following. She knew no one was there—logically, she knew—but the feeling was as real as the pain in her shoulders. Minor surprises, like a door slamming in the hallway, sent her into a full panic, her body bracing for a blow that never came.

Her irritability had grown worse over the years. She snapped at volunteers, she criticized the church secretary, she nearly drove away her closest friend. People began to walk carefully around her, which only confirmed her belief that she was dangerous, that she could not be trusted around others. She had come to believe that the only way to keep everyone safe—herself and others—was to never let anyone get close. Being alone with another person felt like an invisible cage closing in; the exit was not just a door but a symbol of her only chance at escape.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was not the anger or the checklists or the avoidance, but a single moment at the center. A young mother had come in with her toddler, and the child began to cry in a high, piercing way. Layla felt something snap inside her. She turned, walked out the back door, and sat on the curb, her body trembling, the rage so immense she could barely breathe. She could not for the life of her say what the memory was that had seized her—only that the sound of that cry had been a key to a lock she had tried to ignore for fifty years. She called a therapist the next day. She was terrified—terrified that if she opened that door, she would never be able to close it again, and terrified that the rage inside her would consume everything she had built. But she was equally afraid of continuing to live in a world where every closed door felt like a trap, and where the only safety she could imagine was to never stop running.
